summary.title: Testing in the Twenties
summary.one_liner: Tim Bray argues that unit tests are essential, coverage data is worth watching, and integration tests must be fast and reliable, while admitting the evidence for testing is anecdotal.
keywords: how do i test my code
takeaways: Unit tests are an essential investment, and they should run very quickly from a single IDE key-combo.
Watch coverage data for anomalies and changes between check-ins, but don't chase a fixed percentage dogmatically.
For legacy code, write tests when making significant changes to untested functions and never let a check-in lower coverage.
Integration tests must pass fully, be fast enough to run often, and flaky ones should be fixed or removed.
Code reviewers should be able to assume correctness, so tests should demonstrate it before review.
summary.summary: Tim Bray, a long-time infrastructure developer, makes the case that testing culture has been the biggest single contributor to better software in his career and that many teams still under-test. He lists his positions, including unit tests being essential, coverage data being useful, integration tests needing to pass 100% and run fast, and benchmarks belonging in the suite. He openly says there is no high-quality research on testing efficacy, so his claims rest on experience. The post ends with reader comments that debate TDD, private-method testing, and the unit vs integration vs end-to-end terminology.
